extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, taxonomists, and students of scientific classification / philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and practical rules for forming natural groups, constructing scientific nomenclature, and arranging taxa into a natural series to facilitate inductive inquiry. Emphasises choice of characters, the role of types, handling of exceptions, and nomenclatural economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose attributes that give the class marked individuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes should be formed by the attributes which contribute most, either by themselves or by their effects, to render the things like one another and unlike other things; those that give the class the most marked individuality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer attributes that 'fill the largest space in their existence' and would most impress an impartial spectator; these produce what may be called natural groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and adopt distinctions of Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: Every natural classification should recognise and adopt into itself all distinctions of Kind which exist among the objects it professes to classify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To pass over distinctions of Kind and substitute merely definite distinctions would replace classes with more by classes with fewer attributes in common and subvert the natural method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select characters that point to Kinds (not arbitrary characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem is to find a few definite characters which point to the multitude of indefinite ones; characters should be chosen that determine on which side of the barrier of Kind an object falls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These characters should be those which best indicate common parentage or true affinity; if also important in themselves, so much the better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes are determined by characters, not solely by Type
rubrics_metrics.description: Though groups are often suggested by types, a group when formed is determined by characters; it is inconsistent to claim classes are given by type and not by characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A class must possess characters enabling general assertions; reliance purely on resemblance to a type risks missing the true Kind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Type-species as exemplar, not as sole determinant
rubrics_metrics.description: A Type is an example considered as eminently possessing the character of the class and is used as a mental reference; it illustrates the class but does not replace the enumeration of characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The type-species is useful especially when classifying for a special inductive inquiry (choose the species exhibiting the phenomenon most clearly); treat the type as illustrative and convenient for judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow anomalies and imperfect artificial diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural groups often include 'anomalies'—species that transgress the ordinary definition of the family—so diagnoses (artificial characters) are imperfect and are sometimes made to yield to general natural affinities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lindley's 'Anomalies' in families; some genera may lack features typical of the family (e.g., Lowea lacks stipules in Rosaceae). Include near-exceptions when overall affinity warrants it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species (and lower taxa) should be defined by enumerated characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Species are composed of those individuals or plants which possess certain characters selected as marks by which we might recognise the possibility of a common parentage; the enumeration of those characters is the definition of the species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not compose a species merely of things resembling a model specimen; provide a set of characters that together pick out the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: A class is constituted by universal characters and most of those admitting exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: The class is constituted by possession of all the characters which are universal, and most of those which admit of exceptions; exceptions to some characters are made up for by possession of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inclusion is warranted if an object agrees nearly in its known properties with the sum of characters of the class, even if it lacks one or more characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature should convey maximal independent significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific names are defined by the enumeration of characters of the Kind; names should, where possible, indicate by their formation the properties they connote and convey as much information as practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best when the word formation indicates decisive properties (rare); otherwise indicate nearest natural affinities (see binary nomenclature). Names economize memory by reflecting classification hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Binary nomenclature (genus + specific epithet) to express proximate affinity
rubrics_metrics.description: When the distinctive properties are too numerous to indicate in derivation, incorporate into a species-name the name of the proximate natural group (genus) plus a specific epithet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the principle of botanical and zoological binomials; the specific name may reflect one peculiarity, history, or be conventional. Ternary nomenclature (include family/order) is possible but binary is usually sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal nomenclature encodes decisive single property where available
rubrics_metrics.description: When one property alone is sufficient to distinguish a Kind (as chemical composition for compounds), the name ideally should indicate that property (e.g., systematic chemical names indicating composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: French chemists' nomenclature expresses composition and thus gives near-ideal independent significance to names; proportion (stoichiometry) later added.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange kinds into a natural series for particular inductive inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: For investigating the laws of a particular phenomenon, bring into one class all Kinds exhibiting that phenomenon and arrange them in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, from most to least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This facilitates induction by the Method of Concomitant Variations: order instances so that increases or decreases in the phenomenon can be observed across the series (example: comparative anatomy from man down to zoophytes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a type-species when forming a series for inductive study
rubrics_metrics.description: When arranging groups into a series to study a phenomenon, assume a type-species that exhibits the properties constitutive of the class in the highest degree; other varieties are seen as degenerations from that type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The highest-intensity case reveals subsidiary phenomena and collateral circumstances that aid recognition of rudiments in lesser instances; man used as type for animal life in example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary divisions must reflect variations in the degree of the main phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary divisions of a series must be grounded not on all distinctions indiscriminately, but on those which correspond to variations in the degree of the main phenomenon being used as the scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Groups should not be constituted so as to place together things that occupy different points of the general scale; example: break at points where Mammalia ends, where Fishes separate from Insects, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal subdivisions should be contiguous on the general scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Families and genera should, if possible, be subdivided so that one portion stands higher and the other lower on the general scale, preserving contiguity rather than redistributing across the scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only when such subdivision is impossible is it allowable to ground remaining subdivisions on characters not determinable with the main phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: When the principal phenomenon predominates, series-based classification suits general purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: If the principal phenomenon so transcends other properties that it largely determines miscellaneous properties of the objects, then a classification grounded on that phenomenon will often be the most suitable classification for many other inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: animal anatomy and physiology are so central that classifications reflecting the scale of animal life serve broadly for zoological science; beware of undue emphasis on incidental properties (e.g., alimentation).
